newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist leader sharpens campaign rhetoric.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist leader sharpens campaign rhetoric.

text.p: The leader of France's opposition Socialists sharpened his rhetoric on Saturday despite Prime Minister Alain Juppe's plea that the parliamentary election campaign focus on issues rather than personal barbs.

"The balance sheet of our adversaries is bad, their plans are virtually non-existent, but they are content to criticise our ideas. They are behaving like the opposition to the opposition," Socialist Party head Lionel Jospin told a rally in Nailloux, southwestern France.
He spoke a day after Juppe, leader of the Gaullist RPR party, said he hoped to steer the election campaign towards unemployment and other key voter concerns and away from mud-slinging.

"What I deeply desire is for the campaign to change tone," Juppe told France 3 television. "Over the past two weeks it has largely consisted of personal attacks and partisan jibes. The time for such behaviour is over."
All sides in the two-round May 25-June 1 election have been escalating their attacks as polls show the left within striking distance of pushing the governing centre-right out of power.
Juppe may have started it off, pledging at the start of the campaign that it would be both "joyful and brutal".
But the Socialists have not shied from confrontation, hammering away at Juppe, who is unpopular with voters and has come under increasing fire from his own allies for running a lacklustre campaign.

"If this election took place today, based on the popularity of the government and its current leader, there would be no doubt of the outcome," Jospin told supporters. "The question is whether the French people want a new majority."

Despite the new attacks, the outgoing majority was expecting a boost in the polls from this week's written plea by Gaullist President Jacques Chirac to support the centre-right and reject the Socialist alternative.

In an opinion article in regional newspapers, Chirac said his government had had to "wipe the slate clean" after years of Socialist misrule and urged voters to give him the "political stability indispensible for effective action".
Chirac sent shock waves through French politics when he decided last month to hold parliamentary elections nine months early despite a huge majority in the National Assembly.

A win for the centre-right would give it five more years of uninterrupted power, a possibility the left has attacked as a "blank cheque" for more government austerity in a drive to help France qualify for European monetary union.

The Socialists reject Chirac's attempt to blame them for France's record 12.8 percent unemployment, arguing the conservatives have been in power since 1993 and that it is now time to give the left a chance.
The centre-right says it is vital France stay the course to qualify for the single currency and succeed in an era of intensifying global economic competition.

Gaullist Jean-Francois Cope, who helped the RPR draft its economic platform, said one key reason Chirac had dissolved parliament early was to "break with the wait-and-see economic policies that are inevitable during the pre-election period".
Cope called on the next government to reform the civil service and state finances and to cut taxes and payroll charges.
The parliamentary elections were initially set for March 1998, at the same time Europe was due to determine which countries would be eligible for the initial shift to a single currency.
